title: Nyasa: the body made ready
hookLine: before a flower is offered, the worshipper touches their own body with sacred sound
carry: nyasa: the body is part of the altar
tomorrow: the goddess has heard every answer. what does she still want?

cards: Before a free throw, some players run the same small ritual: touch the chest, the shorts, the ball, always in order. Odd, until you see how steady it makes them. Here's an older version that's odder still.
A worshipper sits before the goddess's image, and before a single flower is offered, before the lamp is lit, they touch their own body, place by place, saying a sacred syllable at each.
Why would worship start with your own body?

teach.h: NYASA: PLACING SOUND ON THE BODY.
teach.b: The rite is called nyasa, placing.

In the Mahanirvana Tantra, Shiva walks the goddess through worship step by step, and this comes early: the worshipper places the syllables of a mantra on the body, touching each place as the syllable is said.
Only then does the outward worship begin, the flowers and the lamp. Why start there? Because on this path the body isn't an obstacle to get past.
It's the first place the divine is invited to live.

teach.h: TO WORSHIP A GOD, BECOME DIVINE.
teach.b: Tantric teachers often quote a short saying for it: devo bhutva devam yajet, to worship a god, first become divine. The worshipper isn't a stained thing creeping toward something pure.
They're made fit, a home ready for the deity, before they offer anything at all. And it isn't only for initiates.
Many printed versions of the thousand names of Vishnu, chanted in ordinary homes, open with short nyasa lines, touching the hands and the heart before the names begin.

teach.h: THE BODY: PART OF THE ALTAR.
teach.b: Here the flesh is part of the altar. So the run on the Tantras arrives. A seed syllable and a diagram.
Shiva and Shakti, never apart. A reputation, answered by its own books. A householder's day, offered.
And a worship that begins by touching the body with sacred sound. Not a secret thrill.
A practice, with the whole person in it.

how: Nyasa is part of tantric worship and appears in some temple and home rituals today; the mantras and placements are usually learned from a teacher, often at initiation.

games.q: what does “what tantra actually is” mean?
o: a rite washing the body clean before prayer
a dance performed around the goddess's image
nyasa: sacred sound placed on the body first

games.q: worship begins at home: the body. tap the pairs.
p: placing sacred sound on the body
placed, one place at a time

s: in nyasa, the body is touched to wash away its impurity
it's made ready, made fit, as the first place the divine is invited to live.
in the Mahanirvana's worship, nyasa comes before the outward worship
the body first, then flowers and lamp.

games.q: a friend says every religion treats the body as the problem. what does the nyasa rite suggest?
o: here the body is made ready first, as part of the altar.
she's right: the touching is a way of cleansing something impure.
the body doesn't matter; the touching is just a habit of the hands.
games.why: in tantric worship, the syllables of a mantra are placed on the body before anything is offered. the body is the first place the divine is invited.

practice: Nyasa itself is usually given by a teacher, so try only its spirit. Rest one hand lightly over your heart for a few breaths, then on the crown of your head, then back in your lap.
Let each place be noticed, as if it were being made ready.

wordCard.voice: What tantra actually is: here, nyasa, placing sacred sound on the body before any outward worship begins.

orig.note: Sanskrit nyasa: placing; the rite of placing a mantra's syllables on the body.

carryVoice: Keep this one: nyasa, the body is part of the altar. Worship starts with you. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahanirvana Tantra, chapter 5 (the rite of worship: nyasa of mantra syllables on the worshipper's body before outward worship)
Mahanirvana Tantra, chapters 1 and 8 (the Kali-age frame; the householder), recapped
devo bhutva devam yajet ('to worship a god, become a god'), a maxim widely quoted in tantric and Agamic teaching; attribution varies
Vishnu Sahasranama, preliminary nyasa lines (karanyasa, anganyasa) in common printed recitation versions
